title: Michael Cohen Pleads Guilty to Campaign-Finance Violations
description_medium: On August 21, 2018, Michael Cohen pleaded guilty in federal court in Manhattan to campaign-finance violations and other crimes. He admitted arranging a $130,000 payment to Stormy Daniels and a $150,000 payment to Karen McDougal’s publisher to keep damaging allegations from becoming public before the 2016 election. Prosecutors said the payments were made in concert with the campaign and for its benefit.
description_long:
Michael Cohen, Donald Trump’s longtime personal lawyer and fixer, pleaded guilty in Manhattan federal court on August 21, 2018, to eight counts that included tax evasion, false statements to a bank and campaign-finance violations. In his plea, Cohen admitted arranging two payments before the 2016 presidential election intended to prevent damaging stories about Trump from becoming public. He said he paid $130,000 to Stormy Daniels, an adult-film actor, through a company he created, and helped arrange a $150,000 payment from American Media Inc., publisher of the National Enquirer, to Karen McDougal, a former Playboy model.

Cohen told the court the payments were made “in coordination with and at the direction of” a candidate for federal office. Federal prosecutors later described the payments as intended to influence the election and said the campaign participated. The plea made the hush-money arrangements part of a criminal campaign-finance case, rather than merely private settlements. Cohen was sentenced in December 2018 to three years in prison on the combined federal offenses. His admissions became central to later scrutiny of Trump’s role in the payments, though the plea itself was Cohen’s and did not adjudicate criminal liability for Trump.
evidence_notes: SDNY plea release and charging information establish date, eight-count plea, amounts and Cohen’s account that payments were coordinated with a candidate’s campaign; sentencing release establishes later 3-year sentence. Keep the distinction between Cohen’s guilty plea and charges against other people.

title: DHS Announces Termination of Nicaragua’s TPS Designation
description_medium: On November 6, 2017, Acting DHS Secretary Elaine Duke announced that Nicaragua’s Temporary Protected Status designation would end, citing recovery from Hurricane Mitch. The government set a 12-month transition, with termination scheduled for January 5, 2019. A court injunction later blocked implementation, and DHS rescinded the 2017 termination in 2023. A separate 2025 decision subsequently ended the designation effective September 8, 2025.
description_long:
Nicaragua received Temporary Protected Status after Hurricane Mitch devastated the country in 1998. On November 6, 2017, Acting Homeland Security Secretary Elaine Duke announced that the designation would be terminated. DHS said conditions related to the hurricane had improved and that Nicaraguan nationals should prepare to return or seek another immigration status. The Federal Register notice gave beneficiaries a 12-month transition and set January 5, 2019, as the planned effective date. At the time, roughly 2,500 Nicaraguans were protected under the designation.

The announced termination did not take effect on that date. In litigation brought by TPS beneficiaries, a federal court issued an injunction that kept the designation and related work authorization in place while the case proceeded. In June 2023, DHS formally rescinded the prior termination and extended the designation. A later administration made a separate termination decision in 2025, with DHS reporting that the designation ended September 8 of that year. These later actions are distinct from Duke’s 2017 announcement: this entry concerns the first Trump administration’s decision and its initially planned end date, not an uninterrupted loss of protection beginning in 2019.
evidence_notes: DHS announcement/Federal Register support rationale, transition, planned effective date, and beneficiary count. Ramos litigation injunction kept TPS active; DHS rescinded the 2017 termination effective June 9, 2023. DOJ EOIR 2025 notice identifies separate later termination effective Sept. 8, 2025.

title: Trump Company Reported to Have Spent Money on Cuba Business Trip
description_medium: A 2016 Newsweek investigation reported that Trump Hotels & Casino Resorts paid a consulting firm more than $68,000 for work that included a 1998 trip to Cuba to explore business opportunities. The spending occurred while U.S. restrictions generally barred such travel and transactions without authorization. The reporting alleged an embargo violation; available sources do not establish that the company was fined for it or that Trump personally made the trip.
description_long:
A Newsweek investigation published in September 2016 reported that Trump Hotels & Casino Resorts, the company then controlled by Donald Trump, paid Seven Arrows Investment and Development Corporation at least $68,551.88 for consulting work that included a 1998 trip to Cuba. The consultants reportedly met Cuban officials and business figures to explore possible opportunities for the casino company if U.S. restrictions were later loosened. At the time, the U.S. embargo generally prohibited American companies from spending money in Cuba or conducting unauthorized travel there. Newsweek cited company records and former executives, and reported that a later invoice described the work as related to charity, a characterization experts questioned because it followed the trip.

The report raised allegations of an embargo violation during the 2016 presidential campaign, when Trump publicly supported maintaining the embargo. It was an investigative report about alleged corporate conduct, not a documented federal enforcement action against the company. The linked CNBC URL’s “fined” framing is unsupported by the accessible Treasury enforcement records: a separate 2015 $10 million penalty against the Trump Taj Mahal concerned anti-money-laundering violations, not Cuba. Sources also do not show that Trump personally traveled to Cuba. The defensible account is that reporting alleged his company funded an unauthorized business exploration; the claimed embargo fine should be removed unless a matching enforcement record is produced.
evidence_notes: WLRN/NPR and contemporary reporting summarize Newsweek’s 1998 trip allegation and $68,551.88 company payment. FinCEN’s actual 2015 $10m penalty concerns Bank Secrecy Act/AML failures at the Taj Mahal, not Cuba embargo violations. Source/title appear to conflate separate events.
corrected_wording: Correct title to “Trump Company Reported to Have Spent Money on Cuba Business Trip.” No substantiated federal Cuba-embargo fine appears in the reviewed primary enforcement record; do not present the claim as established.
exact_blocker: The linked CNBC page is unavailable and the available official penalty record is for separate anti-money-laundering violations. A primary enforcement record establishing that the company was fined for a Cuba-embargo violation has not been identified.

title: U.S. Signs Asylum Cooperative Agreement with El Salvador
description_medium: On September 20, 2019, the United States and El Salvador signed an Asylum Cooperative Agreement allowing the U.S. to transfer some non-Salvadoran asylum seekers to El Salvador to pursue protection there. The agreement described a third-country claims process and exceptions for certain people. It never entered into force or operated: the State Department later said the El Salvador agreement was never implemented.
description_long:
The United States and El Salvador signed an Asylum Cooperative Agreement on September 20, 2019, during the Trump administration’s effort to route some asylum claims through Central American countries. Under the proposed arrangement, the United States could transfer certain people who requested protection after arriving at a U.S. port of entry or crossing the border to El Salvador, where they would pursue a protection claim under Salvadoran procedures. The agreement excluded categories including Salvadoran nationals, unaccompanied children and certain people with valid U.S. admission documents. Its operation depended on the agreement entering into force and the receiving country providing a process for protection claims.

The signing did not mean that asylum seekers were immediately transferred or that every person arriving at the U.S. border became ineligible to apply for asylum in the United States. The El Salvador agreement never entered into force and was never implemented. In February 2021, the Biden administration suspended and began terminating the Trump-era Asylum Cooperative Agreements with El Salvador, Guatemala and Honduras; the State Department specifically noted that the agreements with El Salvador and Honduras had never been implemented. The event is therefore the creation of a proposed transfer framework, not a record of completed transfers under this agreement.
evidence_notes: DHS announcement and Senate Foreign Relations hearing establish signing and proposed process/conditions. State Department's 2021 statement explicitly says agreements with El Salvador and Honduras were never implemented. Avoid conflating it with Guatemala’s agreement, which did result in transfers.

title: CDC Issues Title 42 Border Expulsion Order
description_medium: On March 20, 2020, the CDC issued an order under Section 265 of the Public Health Service Act suspending the introduction of certain people from places where COVID-19 was spreading. The Trump administration used the order at land borders to expel many migrants, including asylum seekers, without ordinary immigration processing. Although presented as a public-health measure, the policy’s use and legality faced extensive challenges.
description_long:
On March 20, 2020, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention issued an order under Section 362 of the Public Health Service Act, codified at 42 U.S.C. § 265. It suspended the introduction into the United States of certain people arriving from countries where a communicable disease existed, citing the danger of COVID-19 transmission in congregate border settings. The Trump administration applied the order at the land borders with Mexico and Canada to rapidly return many migrants, including people who otherwise sought asylum, without the ordinary immigration procedures used to assess protection claims. The policy became widely known as Title 42, after the part of the U.S. Code containing the public-health statute.

Civil-rights organizations and public-health experts challenged the policy, arguing that the statute did not authorize expelling asylum seekers and that returning people could expose them to danger. The administration defended it as necessary to limit the spread of COVID-19. Litigation led to exceptions for some groups, including unaccompanied children, while the policy continued through later amendments and extensions. The CDC ultimately determined in 2022 that the order was no longer necessary as public-health conditions changed. The key event was an emergency public-health order that became a major border-enforcement mechanism and sharply curtailed access to asylum procedures during the pandemic.
evidence_notes: CDC archive confirms order issued March 20, 2020 under §265 authority; ACLU supplies context about asylum seekers and challenges; CDC 2022 announcement says the order was no longer necessary. The input linked an unrelated CDC article about Singapore transmission; this uses event-specific sources instead.

title: Trump Announces Revocation of John Brennan’s Security Clearance
description_medium: On August 15, 2018, the White House announced that President Trump had revoked former CIA Director John Brennan’s security clearance. Trump’s statement cited Brennan’s public criticism of the administration and alleged “erratic conduct,” while also asserting that former officials’ access to secrets could be inappropriate. Trump later linked the action to the Russia investigation. Brennan remained a prominent critic of Trump.
description_long:
John Brennan served as director of the Central Intelligence Agency from 2013 to 2017 and became a frequent public critic of President Donald Trump. On August 15, 2018, White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders read a statement announcing that Trump had revoked Brennan’s security clearance. The statement listed what it called “erratic conduct and behavior,” referenced Brennan’s criticism of the administration and argued that former officials who had entered partisan roles should not retain access to sensitive information to support political attacks. It also said the administration was reviewing clearances of several other former intelligence and law-enforcement officials who had criticized Trump.

The action drew immediate debate about whether clearance decisions were being used to punish political speech. Trump later told the Wall Street Journal that Brennan’s role in the Russia investigation was a factor. The White House statement did not allege that Brennan had mishandled classified information, and a group of former intelligence leaders publicly objected to the decision. The announcement concerned Brennan’s access to classified information after leaving government; it did not remove his ability to speak publicly or alter his former role at the CIA. Subsequent reporting questioned when the formal paperwork took effect, so descriptions should distinguish the August announcement from the administrative processing of the revocation.
evidence_notes: Archived White House press briefing includes Trump’s statement and date; Washington Post reporting documents Trump’s remarks linking the decision to Russia inquiry, criticism that the action targeted speech, and question of delayed paperwork. Avoid presenting political retaliation as an official finding.
corrected_wording: Prefer title “Trump Announces Revocation of John Brennan’s Security Clearance” to reflect the August 15 public announcement; later reports disputed when the paperwork completed.

title: Sessions Orders Review of DOJ Police-Reform Agreements
description_medium: On March 31, 2017, Attorney General Jeff Sessions directed Justice Department components to review their policing work, including existing or proposed consent decrees with state and local governments. The memo framed the review around supporting law enforcement and public safety. The department also sought to delay a court hearing on Baltimore’s police-reform decree, raising concern that federal oversight agreements could be weakened.
description_long:
Attorney General Jeff Sessions issued a March 31, 2017, memorandum directing Justice Department components to review their work with federal, state, local and tribal law enforcement. The memo instructed officials to assess collaborative investigations, grantmaking, technical assistance, compliance reviews, task-force participation and existing or contemplated consent decrees, and to ensure they aligned with the administration’s law-enforcement priorities. A consent decree is a court-enforceable agreement that can require a police department to address unconstitutional practices after a Justice Department investigation.

The directive arrived amid pending police-reform cases. The department’s Civil Rights Division asked a judge to delay a hearing on the Baltimore Police Department consent decree, which had been negotiated near the end of the Obama administration. Sessions separately expressed concern that provisions of the Baltimore agreement could limit lawful police powers and reduce safety, while saying DOJ continued to support reform. Civil-rights advocates worried that the review would slow or narrow federal oversight of departments where investigations had found patterns of unconstitutional conduct. The March memo required review; it did not itself repeal every existing decree or establish the later formal standards for consent decrees that DOJ issued in 2018.
evidence_notes: Linked DOJ memo states the broad review directive. DOJ April 7 statement specifies Sessions’s stated objections to the Baltimore decree while expressing support for reform; contemporaneous coverage reports the request to delay court hearing and explains enforceable agreements. Not the separate November 2018 consent-decree guidance.
corrected_wording: Revise title from “Limits” to “Orders Review”; the March 2017 memo directed review rather than categorically limiting or terminating decrees.

title: Trump Says He Wants the Economy Reopened by Easter
description_medium: During a March 24, 2020 Fox News virtual town hall, President Trump said he would “love to have the country opened up” by Easter, April 12. The remark came as COVID-19 spread and stay-at-home measures disrupted daily life and business. It stated his preferred timetable, not a federal order requiring states or businesses to reopen. On April 16, the White House issued phased reopening guidelines for governors.
description_long:
At a Fox News virtual town hall on March 24, 2020, President Donald Trump said he would “love to have the country opened up and just raring to go by Easter,” which fell on April 12 that year. The United States was then in the early phase of the COVID-19 pandemic, with cases rising and public-health guidance urging people to reduce contact. Trump argued that keeping businesses closed for too long could damage the economy, while doctors and officials warned that reopening decisions depended on the outbreak and medical capacity. His comment expressed a goal and did not itself rescind state restrictions or issue a binding federal reopening order.

The remark became part of a broader dispute over how to balance limiting viral spread against economic costs. Trump later said that governors would have authority to make reopening decisions. On April 16, the White House released a three-phase framework based on public-health criteria and intended to guide state and local officials. That later plan did not mean the country reopened by Easter; the administration’s guidelines arrived several days after the date Trump had initially named. The episode captures the tension between his early push to restart economic activity and the continuing need for measures aimed at slowing COVID-19 transmission.
evidence_notes: Archived White House town hall transcript supplies exact remarks and date; April 16 guidelines announcement describes later phased, governor-led framework. This was a stated preference, not a nationwide reopening order.

title: Trump Pardons Oregon Ranchers Dwight and Steven Hammond
description_medium: On July 10, 2018, Trump granted full pardons to Oregon ranchers Dwight and Steven Hammond, convicted of setting fires that burned federal land. Their case drew national attention after a court applied a five-year mandatory minimum and resentenced them to prison. The original sentences sparked the 2016 armed occupation of the Malheur National Wildlife Refuge by supporters protesting federal land policy.
description_long:
Dwight and Steven Hammond, a father and son who ranched in eastern Oregon, were convicted of arson after fires they set spread to federal land. A federal judge initially imposed sentences shorter than the five-year mandatory minimum for the offense, but prosecutors appealed and the Ninth Circuit required resentencing. In 2015, the Hammonds received five-year terms. Their imprisonment became a cause for anti-government activists, and in January 2016 armed occupiers led by Ammon Bundy seized the Malheur National Wildlife Refuge, saying they were protesting federal control of public lands and supporting the ranchers.

On July 10, 2018, President Trump issued full pardons for both men. The White House called their sentences unjust and said an appeal by the previous administration had resulted in disproportionate punishment. Their supporters had argued the mandatory minimum was excessive, while federal prosecutors maintained the fires endangered people and property. The pardons granted executive clemency for their federal convictions; they did not endorse the armed occupation or settle the wider dispute over public lands. The reported date for the pardons is July 10, 2018, rather than May 29, 2018, the date associated with this input record.
evidence_notes: AP/CBS and archived White House statement support July 10, 2018 pardon, federal-land arson convictions and stated rationale. Washington Post reports appeal, five-year resentencing and occupation chronology. The packet's May 29 date is incorrect.
corrected_wording: Correct event date to July 10, 2018; linked AP and archived White House statement both identify this date. Preserve pardon description; the source link originally supplied described unrelated 2019 clemency grants.

title: Trump Signs Deal Reopening Government After 35-Day Shutdown
description_medium: On January 25, 2019, Trump signed a temporary funding measure that reopened the federal government through February 15, ending the 35-day partial shutdown. The deal provided no new money for the border wall he had demanded, but created a bipartisan congressional committee to negotiate border-security funding. About 800,000 affected federal workers were set to receive back pay. The standoff resumed when negotiations failed.
description_long:
The partial federal shutdown that began in December 2018 ended on January 25, 2019, when President Donald Trump signed a short-term spending measure funding affected agencies through February 15. The closure had lasted 35 days, then the longest federal shutdown, after Trump and congressional Democrats clashed over his demand for billions of dollars for a border wall. The temporary deal included no new wall funding. Instead, lawmakers created a bipartisan, bicameral committee to negotiate border-security spending as they worked toward a longer-term budget agreement.

The shutdown had left roughly 800,000 federal employees furloughed or working without pay, and workers were promised back pay when the government reopened. Disruptions had spread to public services and government operations, while unpaid air-traffic controllers contributed to delays at major airports shortly before the deal. Trump announced the compromise in the Rose Garden and said he would pursue other means to secure the border if Congress did not reach agreement. The measure provided a three-week reopening, not a lasting resolution: negotiations later failed, and another funding confrontation followed. The event ended the immediate shutdown without delivering the wall funding at its center.
evidence_notes: Congress.gov confirms enacted short-term appropriations; contemporary reporting provides funding through Feb.15, committee, back pay and worker impacts. Later failed negotiations are context but no precise later shutdown details asserted.
